text: The quantum Fourier transform is, mathematically, exactly the DFT matrix from last lesson — the only new idea is that it now acts on the amplitudes of a quantum state instead of a list of classical numbers, and it has to be built out of a quantum circuit rather than read off a formula.

The defining formula, QFT of j equals one over root N times the sum over k of e to the 2 pi i j k over N times k, is the identical expression to last lesson's DFT. The quantum part is that this output is a superposition, and its coefficients are amplitudes, governed by the rule that squared magnitudes sum to one — which is exactly why the one-over-root-N normalization is mandatory here, where it was only optional classically. Building the QFT means building a unitary circuit that reproduces this exact matrix, not inventing new mathematics.

Here are the exact numbers for a 2-qubit register, N equals 4. QFT applied to ket zero gives the uniform superposition, 0.5 on every one of the four basis states. QFT applied to ket one cycles through the four 4th roots of unity: 0.5, 0.5i, negative 0.5, negative 0.5i — exactly 1, i, negative 1, negative i. QFT applied to ket two alternates plus and minus 0.5 with no imaginary part at all. Every one of these is an exact value, read directly off last lesson's matrix.

The key derivation step rewrites j in binary fraction notation, and with that notation the QFT output factors into a tensor product of single-qubit states — each output qubit carries one phase that depends only on a suffix of j's bits. That's the single most important fact in this chapter: a state that factors this way is exactly the kind a quantum circuit can build directly, one qubit and one controlled operation at a time. If it didn't factor, there would be no shortcut to an efficient circuit at all.
Next lesson turns that product form into an actual, gate-by-gate circuit — the sequence of Hadamards, controlled rotations, and swaps a real quantum computer runs.
